postText:
36% of Americans think China is more advanced at AI than the US. Only 12% think the US is leading. These are Americans talking about their own country.

That number sat with me for a while.

The Pew Research survey also found that 51% of Americans believe AI will increase the gap between rich and poor countries. Only 7% think it'll decrease it. Seven percent.

And then I started thinking about India.

We're one of the largest users of AI tools in the world. But are we having this conversation? Like actually having it, not just the startup Twitter version of it, but the real one. Who's leading, who's falling behind, who gets left out entirely.

The demographic stuff in the survey is interesting too. Americans aged 65 and older are more than twice as likely as 18-to-29-year-olds to say US leadership in AI is extremely important. 56% vs 26%. That generational gap probably exists here too, but I think it runs different in India. Young people here are the heavy users but idk if that translates into policy urgency or just more ChatGPT prompts.

The education gap got me more. People with a bachelor's degree are more likely to believe AI widens inequality between countries, 62% vs 46% for those without one. The people who understand it more are more worried about it. That should tell us something.

India has the users. Genuinely massive scale. But usage isn't the same as shaping.

And we've had our own signals on this. Sarvam AI is probably the most serious homegrown attempt at building foundational AI in India, actually trained on Indian languages, actually trying to own the stack. That matters. But then you also had Ola's AI push, which kind of quietly fell apart. Krutrim got announced with a lot of noise and then just. went quiet. That gap between ambition and follow-through is real and it keeps showing up.

We're consuming this technology at enormous volume and mostly letting other countries decide what it looks like, what it's for, who it serves.

And I don't fully know what the answer is, tbh. More regulation? More homegrown infra? Better public conversation? Probably all of it, probably in the wrong order, probably too slow.

But the 51% number keeps coming back. More than half of Americans, people inside one of the two countries actually racing for this, think AI makes the world more unequal. Not less. More.

If that's true, and I think it probably is, then where does that leave a country like India that's mostly on the receiving end of decisions made elsewhere?

Curious what you think, especially if you've been watching the Sarvam or Krutrim story closely.
